g.passage: By Thursday the water in the cellar had sunk to my ankles, Grandpa Lachlan, so I finally went down with a lantern. Your Gaelic cards were drifting in the corner, and some of the ink had bled into small blue clouds. I sat on the bottom stair longer than I want to admit. Still, our dictionary is only half finished, and you always said a word half learned is a word waiting. I have pinned the cards along the patio line in alphabetical order, the way you would want. Forty can be read; nineteen cannot. I am rebuilding those from memory, and where memory fails I leave a blank square for you to fill when you come home. Señora Ruiz says the damp will lift by Sunday. She has promised to bring her fan down after supper.

When the stationmaster announced that the new Hamburg café would give us a single pastry table, I, Annika, signed the agreement without looking at her. On the first morning she took the left side and I took the right, and she remarked to no one that almond cakes always dry out by noon. By noon, though, her tray had shifted an inch, and my cakes sat in the window light. I said nothing. That evening I left a jar of my almond paste on her side of the shelf, unlabeled. g.passage: Years later, I still remember the frost on the guesthouse windows the morning Aunt Itzel and I had to settle which of us would stay. We owed the brothers a winter of lodging on the plateau, and the abbot had agreed that one of us could work it off through spring. I, Nova, announced that I would stay; I was nineteen, and she had a job waiting in Flagstaff. Itzel did not argue. She asked the abbot about the roof repairs, then about the bread ovens, and wrote both lists in her own hand. When I came back from loading the truck, my duffel was already behind the seat. When the looms of the Tbilisi weaving cooperative fall silent each evening, I set two chairs by the window, and Anushka begins on the tangled yarn the weavers leave behind. We used to play here on Fridays; now nobody asks.
IRENA: You could leave the yarn tonight.
ANUSHKA: (sharply, without looking up) Then what would we do on time?
IRENA: (after a pause) Practice, maybe.
ANUSHKA: Practice for whom?
(IRENA reaches for her violin case. ANUSHKA slides the spool across first, so that IRENA holds one end while she winds.)
ANUSHKA: (still not looking up) Your left wrist again. Rest it on the sill.
(IRENA does. They wind in silence. Neither mentions the hall that cancelled their booking.)
IRENA: Same tempo tomorrow?
ANUSHKA: Slower.
(Outside, a tram rattles past, and the courtyard lamps come on one by one.)

g.passage: Rain dripped from the tin roof of the bus shelter in the hills above Auckland as I buttoned my mother's coat to her chin. I am Tui, and for two years I have been the one who remembers her pills, her appointments, the names of her old friends. This morning she wanted the bus to her church, where the women still save her a seat; I had promised my new manager I would be at the clinic by nine, and my phone buzzed twice in my pocket. My mother did not ask me to stay. She only rested her hand on my arm, a small anchor, and kept her eyes on the road. When the clinic bus came around the bend, I read its number, and I let it pass. Mist slid down the slope and settled over the empty road.

g.passage: Anything to declare? asked Lorenzo, the customs officer, as my mother and I reached the little checkpoint on the Cornish coast, where an old tale says brides once paid their toll in shells. My mother had nothing but a photograph she had found that morning in a box of my grandmother's linens, a box she had not opened in thirty years. It showed her own wedding, the groom's half torn away. I had thought it lost in the flood of '89, she said, and I wanted Callum to see it before we choose the chapel. Lorenzo studied it and waved us through. On the cliff path she told me that the torn-away man had drowned off this coast before I was born, and that the man I call father had married her the next spring. The photograph was a locked chest washed ashore, and I could not decide whether I wanted the key. Gulls hung above the checkpoint roof, motionless against the wind.

g.passage:
I give that relic a week before it burns the place down, CLEMENT says, dropping a basket onto the folding counter of the laundromat in Port of Spain. LINTON, his father, does not answer. He lifts an old charcoal iron from its shelf and sets it heating.
CLEMENT: Nobody pays for hand-pressing anymore, Pa.
LINTON: (smoothing a white collar) Your grandmother pressed shirts for half of Belmont with this.
CLEMENT: (laughing) Because she couldn't afford a machine.
LINTON: (softly) She couldn't. She did it anyway.
(LINTON holds out the iron. CLEMENT hesitates, then takes it. He presses one sleeve, quickly and badly. He lifts the iron, looks at the scorched crease, and dampens the cloth again without being told.)
CLEMENT: How long did she hold it before it stopped hurting?
LINTON: She never said.
(CLEMENT starts the sleeve over, slower this time. Neither of them looks at the washing machines humming along the wall.)

Read the harbor part again, Yuxuan said, so I did, sitting cross-legged among the half-strung kites in the old kite-maker's yard in Lisbon where Mother used to work. Our plan had been simple: sell her last kites at the festival, buy back the letters she had pawned, and learn at last why she left us for three years. We sold all nine before noon. Yuxuan haggled the pawnbroker down by a third and bowed to him like a courtier, and I laughed so hard I dropped the bundle in the street. Tonight the bundle sits on the workbench, retied in her blue thread. She wrote about the harbor, about missing us, about a doctor in Porto she never once mentioned at home. Yuxuan has gone to bed without brushing his teeth. I have put the kettle on twice and forgotten it both times.
Shanice

g.passage: Years later, I can still smell the wet feijoas from the morning the ferry was cancelled and I waited out the rain under a fruit stall at the Auckland market. I was nineteen, and my teacher had just written tidy and empty across the essay I was proudest of. A stranger named Makana sheltered beside me, peeling a feijoa with his thumb. I told him the whole injustice, pausing at the best parts for the outrage I was owed. He asked my name instead. Kian, he repeated, as though trying it on, and then wondered what I would write if nobody graded it. I answered with a twenty-minute speech on fairness, complete with numbered points. I had, I believe, a closing argument. The rain eased by eleven, and the vendors began stacking crates of kumara along the curb.

g.passage: Once, during the spring Haneul rented a farmhouse outside Porto Alegre, her neighbor Taeyang arrived at dawn with a coil of rope and an apology for the noise. He had sailed for thirty years, he said, and his hands still tied knots the old way, even on the fence he was mending for her goats. By summer he had joined the local farmers' cooperative, whose members teased him about his knots and patiently taught him theirs. He practiced their loop on the porch every evening until he could tie it blind. Yet on the gate he trusted most, the one that held the goats at night, Haneul noticed a sailor's hitch, retied fresh each week. In August the eucalyptus shed long strips of bark across the road, and the goats chewed them with great seriousness.
